utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody. Please be seated. Before we continue the line of questions to our current witness, we have to discuss some administrative matters which deserve to be treated with some priority. Yesterday, we received based on the copy of the watch of Mr. Ostojic in time some documents. I think we should take care not to confuse them. In the moment, we are confronted with two expert statements, and I think Prosecution should as soon as possible comment on the question of cross-examination, especially related to the one new proposed statement in writing on the third expert. Pavle Nikolic, Professor Pavle Nikolic which it was sought to be introduced under Rule 94 bis as well. These are not the main problems. The main problem in the moment is the motion of 3 March 2003, defendant Milomir Stakic motion to reconsider the Court's prior decision on experts for leave to amend his witness list. We discussed it a long time yesterday. We compared it with your previous motion. We compared it with what has been described as the parameters for admitting new experts and new witnesses. The motion as such is of a quality that we first have to ask the Defence in all seriousness, do you believe this is a serious motion?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. The motion with respect to our request for experts is indeed serious. And we think it's most serious. We --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Discussing -- reconsider the decision on experts and for leave to amend his witness list where you have a mixum compositum of experts, witnesses, names, nobody knows what the real meaning should be. To be quite frank with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I appreciate that, Your Honour. I can go through it because our subsequent motion to that filing immediately clarified the issue with respect to the two lay witnesses that we wanted to substitute. Initially we were going to incorporate the motion as one. We broke it out. But in that motion we highlight the fact that there will be other witnesses that we will be seeking leave such as the 92 bis witness Dr. Pavle Nikolic as well as the two other witnesses who we specify in a separate motion. But in this motion it was basically giving the Court an overall picture of the three issues that we were mainly concerned with, and just to repeat: One, the experts; two, the substitution of witnesses; and then three the exhibits that we also under separate cover and separate motion sought leave to admit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This Trial Chamber outlined several times what are the parameters for admission of new evidence and amending the witness list. And this is, of course, primarily the question of added value, higher quality, higher experience, and finally relevance. And just to write down the words "pathologist," "exhumation expert," it doesn't help at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I can explain that, Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it should be normally readable from the motion as such. And to be honest, this Trial Chamber is no longer prepared to cure the mistakes of Defence in the past. We did what we could to assist you since December when all these motions should have been brought in. But apparently, they aren't. You are just substituting kinds of experts without making any hint on superior experience, relevance. Just one example, why should we need an exhumation expert, pathologist? And then you had some other -- now you use the term "ethics and procedure amongst others [phoen]" and instead of previously "police expert" now "police academy expert." And then out of the blue, we see a name of a Father Milorad Loncar. Maybe we are wrong based on that what we have heard since the last 126 days, that this person was once mentioned. Unfortunately, we are not aware who is Father Milorad Loncar. So to conclude, in the moment, we can't see the seriousness, and more and more, the motion tends to be frivolous.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may reply, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, we filed a specific application seeking experts in this case. The Court summarily denied our request. Limited the Defence to two, despite the fact that the OTP had numerous experts on with a we considered to be critical points in the fourth amended indictment. Despite, that we disagreed with the Court's decision respectfully, and there was nothing else we could do. The Court invited us and gave us a deadline of Monday to reconsider and if we wanted additional experts to bring it to the Court's attention. We never withdrew our request or our position and we continue to maintain that we have been prejudiced by not having experts which are necessary for this case, specifically with respect to the pathologist, just so that the Court is aware, we cannot at least in the United States of America retain an expert without a retainer before I can actually identify him. So the OLAD will not give us that authority unless the Court grants us that leave. We are caught in a catch-22 where we can't retain an expert, but believe an expert is important. We stress to the Court the superiority of what we consider to be constitutional law experts which the OTP failed to present. We stress to the Court the fact that we need a police expert, whether we call him a police academy expert, someone from the academy himself, or a police expert to determine what the hierarchical structures and duties and obligations were of the policemen in the Prijedor Municipality. We stressed that, and we reiterated solely for the purpose of preserving our right to be perfectly frank with the Court on appeal. The Court's invitation based on the decisional authority clearly states that we must act other than to say that the Court rejected our request. The Court invited us to reiterate our request. We did that. The proffers of those experts we don't have. In order to get their reports, we must pay them. We haven't been given the funds to pay those experts. Clearly we believe on all those issues including exhumation and pathology it's important because the expert or so-called expert Mr. Nicolas Sebire, we heard his testimony, and we can recollect that what the OTP -- how many exhumations they were involved in. And he himself said the standards are different from what the OTP does on exhumations versus what the federation did on exhumations.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sorry. We broke down during his second time he testified after his initial cross-examination, he concluded that out of approximately 270 such exhumations, the OTP was involved in approximately five of them. And then when we further inquired as to what the standards were for exhumations by the Federation, he was unaware of them but felt that his standards, and the standards of the United Nations, and OTP were superior, although he could not explain them. We believe, and we have been in contact with various pathologists who can assist us in evaluating the credibility of this submit and the veracity of the ultimate conclusions that both the Federation and the OTP submit with respect to the pathologist. With respect to the police expert, once again, Your Honour, I have been in contact with three separate police academy officials who can testify, who were willing to testify as early as last summer. I have their resumes, I can find their correspondence. Our request was rejected, so I merely told them they will not be retained in this case. Those experts based on their expertise we hope would have been able to enlighten us since there are specific charges in the indictment, although we strongly feel that the OTP has not proved that. At this stage, since it all passed the 98 bis portion of the case, we believe we have a right and should attack and attempt to refute those allegations in the complaint. Namely, the relationship between the police and the civilian municipal Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. authorities. We believe there has been no evidence of that. But I will not advise my client that therefore we do not need an expert on that issue. Those are the reasons in essence, Your Honour. Finally, with respect to father Milorad Loncar, if I may, his name appears conspicuously for the first time on or motion for leave to obtain certification by the Madam Registrar in our annex. He's an individual who visited Dr. Stakic. We submitted his background report. He's an individual who we believe is a fact witness and also a character witness for Dr. Stakic. We ask that his statement be given via 92 bis. That was rejected. Our application with respect to Father Loncar is simply to have the Court reconsider and admit a 92 bis statement from him which I believe we have now in final form at our apartment or in the alternative to allow us to bring him live so he can testify about the time he met Dr. Stakic, namely in 1992 and in subsequent years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Dear Mr. Ostojic, we have several times we reviewed the transcript, told the Defence what are the prerequisites for the admission of new evidence. And this would be to demonstrate the added value, the superior knowledge, and first of all the relevance. Nothing of this is mentioned in your motion at all. You will receive the answer in writing, but before I just wanted to give you a chance to be heard on the question of seriousness and frivolousness of your motion. You gave your comments, and it's now for the Prosecution to respond. I don't know whether the Prosecution is prepared today already or if the Prosecution prefer as to the seriousness and, no doubt, the Defence is preparing since weeks not this case but preparing the appeal of this case. We are fully aware of this. In the light of this, I think it might be better that we are extremely precise in our words, and therefore submit your response in writing. But, of course, if you have already a statement ready, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I believe that the Defence's candid admission that the purpose of the motion to add the experts is to preserve their rights on appeal goes to the heart of the matter. I think it's very clear that both in the written motion and in the oral arguments that we've just heard, the Defence has failed to show the relevance and the probative value of the offered testimony. So we are very confident that on appeal, the record is very clear that no proffer of the relevance of this evidence has been made and that the Court certainly is not in error in denying this very late request. Admittedly, some of these were asked for earlier, but again a late reiterated request to add experts on issues such as exhumations that are really not at issue in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And finally, we have to ask the Defence, you yourself made the comment that you're acting here as officers of this Tribunal. Please, stick to the truth and don't write in a misleading way that the Office of the Prosecutor called so and so many witnesses or expert witnesses when it was, in fact, a decision under Rule 98. It was the order in part, for example, handwriting expert. It was not the Prosecution asking for this handwriting expert; it was this Chamber ordering the Prosecution to do this work. So please, stick to the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me just reply, Your Honour, to the comment by the OTP and the Court. If I may. If it's not obvious why a police expert is necessary after our exhaustive arguments, no one can compel this Chamber to understand the seriousness of it. The OTP can take a position which it does not. It can withdraw their baseless allegations relating to the nexus between the police and the civilian authorities, or it can set forth for the Court in honesty and in truth what the hierarchy was of the police in the Prijedor Municipality and how it goes to the republic level and ultimately to the federal level. The truth of the matter is they don't have that evidence. Only because they can't produce evidence that there's a nexus. Instead, what they do is to make a bald allegation and hope that no one notices and hope that no experts will be brought forth and hope that it will all go under some sort of cloud of confusion. The constitutionality issues, the Court itself in the transcripts mentioned, referred, and clearly stated in my opinion that it is necessary and important, and invited the OTP to give us the Official Gazette where those constitutional law issues are. What better person than a constitutional law expert to help us understand and get to the truth of what the actual duties and obligations of various functionaries were at the time at issue. Obviously an expert. The Court is suggesting that we offer -- make a proffer. An offer of proof is made at the end of the Defence case. We will if necessary make an offer of proof of what these experts will state. In my motion I clearly state it will not only refute and rebut the allegations of the OTP which we feel are far afield but ours will also show the substantial doubt that exists with respect to what under de jure or de facto the obligations and responsibilities allegedly were of Dr. Stakic. If we didn't have de jure, I could understand the position of the OTP. If we didn't have joint criminal enterprise, I could perhaps understand their position. If we didn't have widespread and systematic attack, perhaps we could understand and pare down the list of experts in order to establish that. Instead, they throw all these alternative and multi-crooked theories and leave it for us to try to understand and to obtain experts on that. We cannot bring an expert without having leave of Court and payment to retain that expert. I can identify the experts, truthfully to the Court who contacted. We can identify for the Court specifically those individuals. The Court denied our request --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry, but now you are overstepping. You are really overstepping, Mr. Ostojic. You know that it was your duty since at least November last year, and you failed to do the necessary what a Defence should do in this trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, with all due respect, and I apologise if the Court feels I overstepped, the Defence made an application --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No, I don't want to hear any longer these submissions. You repeatedly and repeatedly and misleading the public by stating that you had no chance. You failed to do what was necessary, and you yourself admitted that you failed. And all the time we used to cure that what you failed to do, and please don't come now after the deadline and complain about all the assistance we gave not the Defence but Dr. Stakic, because this case is on Dr. Stakic and not on Mr. Ostojic and not on Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may just clarify, Your Honour, with respect to what I perceive as the Defence counsel's failings it was on the specific proffers and statements of summaries. However the misguidance that we had were based on other Chambers and what was accepted there. We do appreciate the Court's assistance and the patience by the OTP with respect to those. We do not agree, and I do not personally agree, that the Defence failed in their obligations respectfully in any manner in this case. I can cite, and I'm not trying to be misleading at all, I know how many experts were called by the OTP, how many in-house witnesses were called by the OTP. We made our request. We're not going to go back and reiterate the request. We have to live with the decision --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, we are not in kindergarten here saying the Prosecution has ten witnesses and therefore you have also the right to have ten witness. They have three experts and then you have the right to --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This is the content of your motions. The quality, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's not. But I think it's necessary because we have principles and we have in the actual statutes equality of arms is always mentioned. The Court mentioned it themselves. It's perhaps my misunderstanding what that means but equality of arms means that we will both be able to go in there on the same playing field, on the same basis with the same amount of resources available to us. We were not given Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that. I am not trying this case for appeal. I am confident, and I am saying this very truthfully to the Court, that this Trial Chamber at the end of the day, when you review and revisit the testimony of the witnesses that were proffered here, you will find in favour of Dr. Stakic. I'm very confident of that. I am not trying this case on appeal. I resent the comments by the OTP that I am. However, as a lawyer, I'm obligated to preserve my rights and to preserve the rights of my client. I think that this Court will find in favour of Dr. Stakic on all those counts. Why we didn't get it earlier, I don't know. I believe that if the Court examines all the witnesses, once again, you'll find that they are -- the witnesses offered by the OTP on critical essential elements such as widespread and systematic, they will find that there is absolutely no evidence of that, none whatsoever. Therefore, they fail in their burden of proof. So I'm not trying this case on appeal, and I don't want anyone to think that we did. The Defence I think has done a remarkable job based on the resources given to us. We once again appreciate the Court's patience with us, and the Court's assistance when it came to the proffers and other issues. On the experts, it takes six to nine months to retain these individuals. There's an enormous amount of material. Once the Court denied our request, we were left with just proceeding with the two and working to obtain those and that's the issued that remained. We didn't understand why the Court reinvited us to present the expert issue, we thought it was a moot issue at that point. So in order to preserve, and at the Court's invitation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Once again, I have to interrupt you. This is not the truth. Since it's reflected on the transcript, since our first statement related and decision related to witnesses and experts, we clearly expressed our view that when the Defence, if the Defence feels necessary to hear additional experts, then they have to demonstrate the criteria set out before and already at that time. So let's conclude this dark chapter of this hearing. A final question to the Defence: Yesterday, Mr. Lukic was kind enough to tell us that you would search for a replacement of the witnesses 055 and 083. I think the one is related to replacement of the priest, but until today, we don't know. You just mentioned this priest once visited Dr. Stakic. We don't know when. We don't know where, what's it about, what about the relevance? What about the second witness to be replaced? We can't find anything on this in the motion. We can't wait for this. May I ask the Prosecution, are there any comments on the four filings pursuant to Rule 94 bis as of yesterday related to Mr. Nikolic, General Dumat [phoen], and Dr. Trifkovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We just received the filings, and we have not yet received the expert reports ourselves, the OTP. Just one comment on the motion for leave to amend the witness list, the two witnesses given at least on what I was just handed, there's no indication of what they will testify to, no proffer. I don't know if the Defence has a proffer. But in order to add witnesses at this time, I presume that they have some idea of what relevant evidence the witnesses will be adding. I don't know if that's available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But this has to be demonstrated, and it's not yet demonstrated. Therefore, in the moment, there is nothing to decide. We expect additional comments by the parties, taking into account that the deadline was set for yesterday. Anything else for the moment on administrative measures? This is not the case. May I then ask the usher to escort the witness into the courtroom, please. Finally, I'm grateful that Madam Registrar gave me the hint, Prosecution reserved the right to comment on the one additional 92 bis statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes. The testimony that was offered, we have no objection to that 92 bis statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then this is admitted into evidence. Madam Registrar, the number --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Perhaps we should specify --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I just wanted to have the number from Madam Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 74.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And then there was a request for the admission of a transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, as to 74, we have no objection to the admission of that transcript under Rule 92 bis and do not seek to cross-examine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence as such. So, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Budimir. Your headphones are functioning; you can hear me. So please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Questioned by the Court: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask you, did you have any contacts with any of the parties or any other witness by chance since we met yesterday?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not have any contact with the parties or witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then we can proceed immediately. And may I, having reviewed yesterday's transcript, may I ask you in order of taking into account the limited time available for us to answer briefly if possible. Yesterday, when I make reference to the transcript, please don't be confused because it's only for the parties and for the transcript that when later we are coming back to the transcript of another day, we can find where you made this statement. So I want to follow up with that what was said yesterday on page 70, 7-0. We discussed Crisis Staff, working of the Crisis Staff. And my question was, line 3: "Was there any separate group within the Crisis Staff holding separate meetings, maybe as often happens in political circles, inner circles?" Your answer was: "As regards informal meetings and the internal side of its work, I can't remember that Mr. Stakic socialised with Mr. Drljaca. He socialised with Mr. Travar and me, but he socialised more with Mr. Arsic, Simo, and especially with Mr. Kovacevic." Sorry for my omission of yesterday not to ask you, Simo, when you mentioned "Simo," what would be the second name of this Simo? We have a lot of Simos as acting persons in this case.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you allow me to comment, I don't know whether the translation was good, but I think that the first part of the statement that you repeated does not correspond to what I said. I said that Mr. Stakic -- I said that I do not dispute that Mr. Stakic socialised more with Mr. Arsic, Mr. Drljaca. Specifically, this relates to Mr. Simo Drljaca. And that he socialised less with myself and Mr. Travar, and I also said that Mr. Travar and I mostly spent time receiving and processing information which we received from the civilian sector which was then passed on to the staff. This top part would suggest as if he socialised more with myself and Mr. Travar, but actually it was with Mr. Arsic and Mr. Drljaca that he socialised with more. In informal and daily contacts, Mr. Stakic spent much more time with them than he did with me and Mr. Travar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So I don't want to give you the answer of my question. My question was when you mentioned yesterday "he socialised more with Mr. Arsic, Simo, and especially with Mr. Kovacevic" just to fill in there, what was the second name of this Simo you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Drljaca, Drljaca. I said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I didn't want to put it on your tongue. Therefore, this second question. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Were Mr. Arsic, Mr. Drljaca, Mr. Kovacevic, and Mr. Zeljaja also members of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Arsic and Mr. Zeljaja were not members of the Crisis Staff while Mr. Drljaca and Mr. Kovacevic were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did Mr. Arsic and Mr. Zeljaja attend meetings of the Crisis Staff on a regular basis?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that they attended regularly. They were there occasionally, there to discuss certain questions that were discussed at the Crisis Staff meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Who attended, Mr. Arsic, Mr. Zeljaja, or both?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first part of the work of the Crisis Staff was something that Mr. Arsic attended, and then Mr. Zeljaja attended later. I think there was some kind of an organisational change in the functional sense relating to the duties they were carrying out. So this was probably the reason why Mr. Arsic was replaced by Mr. Zeljaja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What was your, and especially where was your office during the entire year of 1992? Yesterday you mentioned the building where you worked initially in April, May. Was there any change?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: During that time period that you are talking about, I worked at the building across the street from the Municipal Assembly building where the ministry for internal affairs and the municipal secretariat for national defence were located. And later, that was reorganised into the Defence ministry of the municipality of Prijedor. I'm talking about that period. Later, during the war, the Ministry of Defence, the department of Prijedor, relocated to a different part of the town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Isn't it true, sir, that - maybe there's a misunderstanding - that your office during 1992 was in the municipal building?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, my office in the course of 1992 was in the building across the street from the municipal building where the ministry for internal affairs was. In another part of the building, in an annex, the Ministry of Defence was located, and that's where the secretariat was for national defence, and that is where my office was. All duties from the jurisdiction of the organ that I headed were performed in that place, and that's where all the staff was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Maybe it assists you when I put to you what you said at the meeting in the hotel, together with Mr. Koumjian. There, you were asked on page 41 by Mr. Koumjian: "Was your office during 1992 in the municipal building?" And then you said: "In the municipal building?" Mr. Koumjian asked: "Yes." And then once again you said: "No, no." So your testimony would be that it was only when you were on the -- on duty, and please correct me if I am wrong, that only when you were on duty - and yesterday you mentioned that you took this work extremely seriously, and therefore you were often on duty - that then you worked in the basement of the municipal building. Would this be correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allow me to be precise. The work hours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Was from 7.00 a.m. to 3.00 p.m., and that period I spent at my workplace at the premises which I talked about a little earlier in the ministry of the internal affairs i.e., in the annex of that building where the municipal secretariat was located. That's where I spent my work time, from 7.00 a.m. to 3.00 p.m. After that, I had a short break, it was an hour or two depending on the time and my family obligations. Since at that time I was living in a village which was about 6 kilometres away from town, so occasionally I would go home. Upon my return to town, I would go to the premises of the centre for reporting where all the information from the civilian sector was collected and which were processed and then passed on to the Crisis Staff for review and resolution of the problems that had cropped up in the civilian sector in the town. So these were my movements, my work hours during the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You mentioned once again unfortunately only the premises of the centre for reporting. But this centre was located in the basement of the building of the Municipal Assembly. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, undoubtedly, they were in the basement of the Municipal Assembly building. This was located there before the events, after the events, and to this very day, the centre is still in the same location. And all the equipment and the technical means that are required for it to work are located there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Whom would you meet there during your shift? Let's limit it to members of the Crisis Staff first.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before that, I have to say that the people who worked there were from the organ that I headed. They maintained the shift, maintained contacts, received the information, wrote them down. But as far as the members of the Crisis Staff are concerned, and I've said that before, other than myself, most of the time that was spent there was spent by Mr. Travar in view of the nature of the information which were received and processed. I'm not ruling out the possibility that all the other members of the Crisis Staff also came there. In exceptional circumstances, it would also be somebody from the military. But this was only dropping by for about half an hour or so to see what was going on, whether there were any problems in town and so on. Otherwise, the other members went there of the Crisis Staff as well as Mr. Travar, who would spend two to three hours there while the others would only stay there from half an hour to an hour and did not stop by every day, but did so depending on their duties and if they needed to stop by and to find out what types of information were arriving at the reporting centre. And I am saying this relating to the military and the police because their communication centre was separate. They had independent communication centres for their own needs. This was exclusively a centre for the civilian needs, for the needs of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would you meet there Dr. Stakic, Mr. Dragic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, occasionally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Dragic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember whether Mr. Dragic went there in the functional sense. There was no need for that and I believe that he didn't really drop by there. I don't remember noticing anything like that, perhaps on a couple of occasions but I don't remember that. I'm not ruling out the possibility that he did drop by, perhaps I wasn't there at the time. But I don't remember anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Transcript is frozen, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry, I can't control everything at the same time. Is it a serious technical problem or...? No, I think we are fine again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We did miss the last I believe -- it did come out. Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Technical miracles happen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not a technical expert, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It's safe so...

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Is that true? I don't see Mr. Dragic's name?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It's only in part. So let me repeat. The question was would you have seen Mr. Stakic, Mr. Dragic there?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I would see Mr. Stakic, that he did drop by occasionally to the premises of the reporting centre. But I don't remember Mr. Dragic coming. I'm not ruling out the possibility that he was there at the premises, but I think that in the functional sense, he didn't need to be there. I don't know whether he dropped by informally and perhaps talked with somebody there. I'm not ruling out that possibility in view of the fact that I did not spend all of my time there at the premises.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I just ask, did you discuss with Mr. Dragic his own testimony here in The Hague during the last four weeks?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did have informal contacts with Mr. Krejic and Mr. Dragic, but Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. this was with coffee in a restaurant, so we didn't go into any details. I just asked them how they felt and how did it go. But I didn't discuss anything with them in details. And they didn't show any willingness either to talk about that topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you remember playing cards together with Dr. Stakic in this centre?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't play cards. I don't know that much about cards. As far as card playing goes, I know some very simple games, but I don't know gin rummy or any other games. So I'm not ruling out the possibility that they did play cards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. And this brings me to the next question, what is "they"? Who else appeared there? Would Mr. Drljaca, Mr. Srdic, Mr. Zeljaja appear in their coordinating functions as set out in the rules on the establishment of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if the rules provided for them coming to the reporting centre. I think that as far as Mr. Srdic and Mr. Zeljaja came by very rarely. Mr. Drljaca stopped by occasionally, just like Mr. Stakic, to the premises of the reporting centre, if this is what we're talking about. Because you had said "they," so I wasn't quite sure exactly who and where.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You have answered this question because I wanted to know what is "they" in your last answer. But let's now concentrate, please, on the meetings of the Crisis Staff, the formal meetings of the Crisis Staff, as such during this relatively short period Crisis Staff replaced other organs, especially at this period of time when there was no meeting of the Municipal Assembly. The decisions taken in the Crisis Staff, were they taken unanimously or with majority or with a qualified majority?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you specifically. I think the decisions of the staff were not adopted by a vote, a majority, or so on. It was a discussion which was concluded at the end, the question was asked whether anybody had anything to add or to rule out relating to the topic that was discussed. There was no vote. There was no raising of hands. There was no affirmative vote. Mostly, it was discussion on a certain topic, perhaps we voted very rarely. I'm not ruling out the possibility that there was an occasional vote. But the actual way we worked was to this effect. Even when we were formulating the agenda, I believe that there wasn't a precise agenda. There was a broad item, political security situation. And within that item, all of the different questions were discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What was then the procedure once a decision taken? What would be the next step with this decision?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: By adopting a decision, a conclusion, or any other document which the Crisis Staff was performing in view of the fact that it had taken over the functions of the Municipal Assembly, which was not able to function, then the way a decision would be implemented or formed or if it would be forwarded to other legal entities. This was something that was managed by the expert service or administrative service of the Municipal Assembly which served the Municipal Assembly. If and when the Municipal Assembly was not working, this expert service was working for the Crisis Staff. So I don't know exactly how these decisions or other conclusions or documents that were adopted at the Crisis Staff were processed further. I had information only about the duties that I was performing. I shaped only one regulation as far as I remember. I participated in its preparation and adoption, and it related to the introduction of 24-hour duty in the Crisis Staff. And I think I talked about that earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right. Take this example: Did you receive later the decision taken in a formal way, this would say, in a signed and stamped way, that you would have a basis for the implementation of this decision?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't, at least I didn't receive decisions in a formal written form. Any decisions that would be relative to what was discussed and considered at the session of the Crisis Staff. Maybe I have a slight disadvantage, and that is that I see these decisions for the first time. And as far as I know, they were ratified by the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor, all the decisions made by the Crisis Staff. But due to the nature of my job, I did not attend that session of the Municipal Assembly where these decisions were ratified. But given my job in the inspection and state administration, when I talk about the formality of these decisions from the formal and legal point of view, as you said, I don't want to discuss that. This is something that I find surprising. I don't know why these decisions were worded in this way, why they were shaped in this way. It is up to the secretary of the staff or the president of the Municipal Assembly who was supposed to implement the decisions without derogating the prevailing laws, so it was not up to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Within the Crisis Staff, who played the leading role?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: By his function, the president of the Crisis Staff, Mr. Stakic, presided over the sessions of the Crisis Staff. He was the one who chaired the sessions, and he channelled the discussion on various issues that were discussed at the sessions. I'm not talking about power; I'm talking about the leading role in the Crisis Staff. As for the further dispersion, this is not relevant to what I was talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's stick, in fact, to facts. And therefore, the question, it's true that Dr. Stakic not only in theory but also in practice presided over the meetings of the Crisis Staff. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you ever visit Dr. Stakic in his office in the municipal building?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only when I had to talk to him about my job and only when I had to discuss matters within the purview of the secretariat that I headed. It was not very often in that period of time. I don't remember exactly how many times it was, but I believe it was two or three times that I went to his office to discuss the matters pertaining to my area of competence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you go directly to his office, or did you make an appointment previously?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no formal need to schedule an appointment, but in any case, given our mobility, mine and the president's, we did make a prior contact. But it was not a formal announcement. I would just call him to see when he was free. Then he would tell me: "Come in 10 or 15 minutes. I have some people sitting in my office. And then when they leave, you can see me." So I didn't have the need to make any formal announcement. I would just go to see him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would you call him directly or through his secretary?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I used the secretary's number. That number I knew because I had used it all the time, even Dr. Stakic was out of the office. The secretary was always there. That's why I used her number. I did not know his direct number. I never used it as far as I remember. In addition to telephone numbers, there was some functional numbers with three digits. And those were direct lines between the president of the municipality, the chief of SUP. But those we used very rarely. I don't remember that we ever used it because our communication was at such a level that we could work normally. There was no need for us to use those functional connections, connections between various functions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you also have access to this three-digit contact numbers or functional numbers, you used this term?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did have access to them. In my office, the number was 132. The president or other people had 134. There were seven or eight such numbers and telephones. But people never got used to using those numbers. And I was no exception. I really didn't use those three-digit numbers at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did Dr. Stakic, when you met in the Crisis Staff, often express a dissenting opinion or protest against the one or Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. other decision taken by the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've told you that the Crisis Staff did not really make decisions. We usually discussed current issues. We tried to reach consensus on what should be done. There was no voting or making decisions as such. During those discussions, there were different opinions heard from those who attended the sessions. And I believe that Dr. Stakic also expressed some different opinions. He had, to put it this way, he would get into some sort of conflicts when discussing things with Mr. Drljaca. But unfortunately, I can't comment on that part, on that relationship, because I don't know what these people knew, what information they had. So I didn't have the same information. It would be wrong for me to pass a judgement on any of these discussions between these two individuals, between Dr. Stakic and Mr. Drljaca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This leads me to the next question. Do you recall a special incident that a group of members of the Crisis Staff being not SDS members put forward a proposal to try to form a special unit because of the abuses there were being carried out by some military and police authorities in Prijedor, a special unit to control those? Do you recall this?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that we touched upon that yesterday. And I said when there were problems in town, when they increased, when they could no longer be contained by the army and the police, and when the Crisis Staff started talking about the situation in town, about order and plundering and killings, then there would be conflict regarding the authority of the police and the authority of the army. The army was supposed to control the movements of all the conscripts and military personnel, and the police was to -- supposed to keep order among the civilians. And when we asked from the chief of the police to introduce some order into town, he would just say that he couldn't do that because everybody in town was wearing uniforms and that they should be under the jurisdiction of the army. Then the army would say that they controlled their men and that the unruly behaviour should be ascribed to the civilians, not to the army. And what remained as a question was who was it that behaved in that way? We would reach a dead end when we discussed those questions. And when that situation culminated, we asked about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I asked you about a very concrete incident; let's call it maybe even a dispute, maybe even between Dr. Stakic and Mr. Drljaca, on a very concrete issue of abuses carried out by military and police authorities, and there was a proposal to form such a special unit. Isn't that true? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. But I just wanted to give you a more elaborate introduction. I apologise. Sometimes I go into too many details, but I believe that it is in the interest of this Court to explain things. So let me be more direct. So when these things culminated, then the Crisis Staff was asked to prevent all that because the army and the police couldn't do that. Then there was a requirement to form a new, special unit, and there was a suggestion that came from the Crisis Staff and from the president of the municipality that people should be appointed to a new unit and that everybody in the Crisis Staff should appoint one honest person who would be a member of that new unit. A discussion followed, and the army and the police did not allow the Crisis Staff to interfere with the way decisions were being made, and they said that the Crisis Staff should not interfere with the appointment of these people because it should be under the exclusive authority of the police and of the army. A verbal conflict followed. And finally the Crisis Staff did not have a say in the forming of that unit. It was the police and the army who had an independent say in the setting up of that unit. And as a result of all that nothing was achieved. We couldn't do anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned just briefly "everybody in town wore uniforms." May I come to the question, did you yourself wear a uniform and pistol, and in which period of time?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that everybody wore uniforms in town, but that the majority of people were assigned either to the police or to the army. We're talking about 70 per cent of the people who were engaged either in the police or in the army, and the remainder of the able-bodied men were either in the civilian protection or had work obligation. Those who were in the army and the police did wear a uniform. As for me personally, I did wear a uniform for a short period of time, and I had my own personal pistol, a small 765 Bereta pistol. But to be honest, I didn't like that. This was my position. I'm just a foot soldier. I didn't have a rank. And my attitude towards the army and towards all that was not one of strong inclination toward that. I was offered to join the army, to be given a rank, but to this very day, I have remained a foot soldier and I have never really wished to join the army. This was just not something I've been attracted to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Understandable. Could you please be a little bit more concrete. When did you receive a uniform and pistol and by whom?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The pistol that I carried was my own pistol. And as for the uniform, I received that because somebody had ordered those uniforms. Either it was a secretary of the economy or somebody else, and that's how I got it. And later on, I received uniforms from the army and from -- I don't know. When we went to make rounds of military units, we had to wear a uniform because it was part of my job description. I was supposed to wear a uniform. And it was my official duty to have a Heckler pistol in my office. I kept it in a safe in my office. This pistol had been obtained by the head of that organ, and that pistol had been kept in the office. I never used it. There was no need for me to use it. It is a big, ugly piece of weapon. And maybe only when I went to inspect war units I would carry that piece of weapon. But that was on really very rare occasions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You mentioned previously you received uniforms from the army and from -- you said: "I don't know who would be this person." Can you try to recall who was in charge of distributing uniforms? Because based on the testimony of several persons we heard here, apparently a number of persons wore uniforms at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Somebody from the Executive Board. Whether it was the vice-president or the president or maybe the secretary for economy. I believe that it should have been their job. Whether it was Mr. Travar or Mr. Dragic, they were the ones who were involved in the procurement and the obtaining of these because these had to be paid for. I really don't know they obtained uniforms from. I believe it was from a Prijedor-based textile factory. But I really wouldn't be able to tell you more about the circumstances of how the uniforms were obtained and who they were obtained by.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's try to fix the exact point in time by some incidents. Was it immediately after the takeover, say, the 30th of April?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that it was in the period between May and June. But to be more precise on that, it is very difficult for me to remember. I believe that it may have been in May, but I really cannot be precise. I can't even give you the part of a specific month when it happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So it would be your testimony it was not related to any concrete incident happening at that time in Prijedor Municipality. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. Given the nature of my job, it would be very difficult for me to be precise on the way uniforms were obtained. At that time, I just didn't find it important, and I didn't think it would be important for me to pay any attention to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And may I finally ask, who was it that gave you the additional Heckler? I know it's a heavy weapon.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody gave me the Heckler. The Heckler was simply sitting in my office in the safe. And that piece of weaponry was obtained before any of the incidents had happened. So while there was still the League of Communists and when the secretary of that organ was a different person, then weaponry was obtained for all the secretaries of various secretariats. Some of these weapons had been returned, and some had remained in the offices. So nobody gave me the Heckler. I just found it sitting there in my office when I was appointed to my position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And did you need any certificate for your pistol?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I had a license for my pistol. I got it from the competent body. This pistol was my private property. I had had it before any of the incidents took place. So I didn't need any additional license. As for the second piece of weaponry, this was an official pistol that I had in my office, if that is what you're asking me about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did everybody or did all the members of the Crisis Staff at this certain period of time wear uniforms and pistols?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of the members of the Crisis Staff, at least for a short period of time, wore uniforms. I'm talking about the stormy period when all the incidents took place. It was not a prescribed obligation, so everybody did it according to their own decision. There was no obligation. Some people wore civilian clothes; the others wore uniform for a longer or shorter period of time. Every member of the Crisis Staff made their own decision on wearing a uniform. So some wore it for a longer period of time; some for a shorter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did Dr. Stakic wear a uniform and a pistol?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for a certain period of time. But I believe that he was also one of those who had taken off the uniform quite quickly and changed into civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did the Crisis Staff change the name, or just in the form of a leading question, was there ever a change to "war presidency" and/or "war commission," and why was this?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, later on I did see a decision made by the president of the state about the establishment of the war presidency. And I believe that this is relevant to that particular period of time. I don't know whether a war commissioner was appointed later on. But during the period when this staff was active, I can't remember the exact period of time when this presidency was appointed. I don't think -- I think that there was some sort of a gap, a time gap, in all these events. I don't know what the regulations were at the time, whether these regulations were amended, whether the decision came from the president. But as far as I can remember, there was no particular session at which the Crisis Staff would be officially reappointed as a war presidency. I only know that later on when sessions continued taking place, that those were the sessions of the National Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So it would be more or less a mere change of name and no change of members, and no change of the work? You can see it reflected on the Official Gazette, that once it was called "Crisis Staff" and then later on "war presidency." But de facto, it was no difference. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you're saying is correct, but I don't remember that it was ever discussed at any of the sessions, that the change of name was on the agenda of any of the sessions, that this body was ever officially renamed. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And then one final question when reviewing your testimony of yesterday, what about a so-called option 2 government? You can hear? Okay. Fine.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, I can. At the beginning I did not have the sound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So to start again: Could you please explain to us the meaning of that what we heard previously under the notion of "option 2" government as of January 1992. What does this notion "option 2" government mean?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must repeat that during that period of time, I was not close to any of the parties. I did not have any insight into this matter, the matter that you're talking about, the establishment of the second option government during 1992. I really don't have any information on that. Therefore, I cannot answer your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The trial stays adjourned until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Only during the last break we received defendant Milomir Stakic's motion for leave to amend witness list. As to the unclarity of this motion, I have to ask the Defence, they make the statement under point 1: "Stakic Defence wishes to use in lieu of three prior witnesses the following witnesses..." Who are the three prior witnesses who are for various reasons unavailable to participate in the trial proceedings in this case that we have the transcript -- the record correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm not sure why the Court received that only during the break. We filed it yesterday with a number of other exhibits -- or motions. But that's neither here nor there. The witnesses which we would replace are 034, who we cannot locate as we advised the Court, I think a couple of weeks ago that we kept looking for, and are unable to locate and maintain contact with him. Also --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. And also Witness 055, the Court assisted us, as you may recall, in having the OTP provide us with information because we did have contact with the witness at one point, and then we've lost contact, and it was based upon information and belief that he left the area. The OTP provided us with his full name, his date of birth, his father's name, and generally that he's living in the Prijedor Municipality. We didn't have a specific address or a phone or other contact number, so it would be for those two witnesses that we would be asking the Court's permission to substitute the two that we identify in our motion to amend the witness list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Surprisingly enough that you are not able to have the phone number of this witness you can read in the phone book of Prijedor. But okay, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The point being, Your Honour, the phone book isn't published daily. That phone number that we had, we did establish contact, and the Court invited us to get the most recent information from the OTP, and they didn't even have the address of the witness. So we were left with not being able to contact this witness any further. If the Court has information and they contacted him at that number, the number that we have from the phone become is no longer being responded to by this individual. So...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It was only yesterday that we learned by the current witness that this witness would commute from Prijedor to Belgrade because the family is living in Belgrade. Okay. 055. And the third one would be?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] We believe the third one would be, Your Honour, 025.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. My mike was off. 025.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then under 3, you mentioned two names. Is it correct that maybe some -- we all make mistakes, that there is an attachment missing on the issues and -- or a proffer what they are -- these witnesses are expected to testify about? Is there any such attachment?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That attachment was not attached, so it was not a mistake that the Court doesn't have it. We're in the process of preparing and completing that for the Court. We don't have one prepared at the present, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We hope to get that to the Court by the end of the week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In addition, we received also only during the last break defendant Milomir Stakic's motion to admit written statements of Professor Pavle Nikolic under Rule 92 bis. Is it correct that you want to introduce the statement of this expert under Rule 92 bis?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the rules seem to suggest that the report is under 94 bis as we've introduced the other two experts. Since we didn't have leave of Court for this individual, we are asking that it simply be admitted under 92 bis as a statement like we have some prior statements that were introduced. As I think we outlined in our motion, that has previously been accepted and identified as an exhibit in a different Trial Chamber. That may not have any weight. I'm not suggesting it does or doesn't. I'm merely providing that information to the Court. And we would be asking that statement be brought in, although I thought we covered it this morning, be admitted in as evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The question what should be the legal basis, Rule 92 bis or Rule 94 bis?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, first we would have to have leave of Court, so we're asking that we get leave of Court to introduce this witness. And then we won't be calling him live, so therefore, we would be requesting after filing it under 94 bis that it be accepted under 92 bis as his full statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The Prosecution reserved the right to comment on this. We then will let you decide on this. May I ask the usher to escort the witness into the courtroom, please. Thank you. We are about to conclude the issue of Crisis Staff as such. Just to cover the entire area of decisions made by Crisis Staff, would it be for the Crisis Staff to issue permits for movements?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who do you mean? Whose movements? Who does that refer to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Individuals or citizens, say, of Prijedor, or would this be for the --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this was not in the jurisdiction of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Movement on the territory of the municipality was not in the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Defence either. This was in the jurisdiction of the ministry for internal affairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask the usher to show the witness Exhibit S126B. And also today, please, the English version on the ELMO and the B/C/S to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We don't have an English version, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please put the B/C/S version on the ELMO, and may I ask the witness to work with the ELMO. I know it's not that easy, but... Could you please explain to us what you can read there.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It states: "Permit for movement issued by the public security station of Prijedor." And it's signed by Mr. Simo Drljaca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can you identify the stamp?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can identify the stamp. It's the centre for security of Banja Luka, public security station Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: On the top, there you can read the ministry having issued this document. Could you please read out what we can see on the headlines on the top of this document.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, ministry for internal affairs Sarajevo, Security Services Centre Banja Luka, public security station Prijedor." This was a unified organ on the territory of the republic, and these are just lower organisational unit of the unified body of the ministry for internal affairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Was this the rule that such a document would be issued on the level of Prijedor and why this?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about the rules from the jurisdiction of the public security station or the ministry for the internal affairs. I didn't have access to such regulation, so I really couldn't say based on what regulations this permit for movement was issued.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you yourself have such a permission for movement?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And why was it that Mr. Beglerbegovic needed such a permit?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Have you ever discussed in the Crisis Staff the need of having a permit for movement?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, from the meetings that I attended, I don't remember any discussion about limiting movement or about permits for movement for certain citizens. I don't know. However, whether bodies who had that in their jurisdiction from the ranks of the police or the army dealt or issued such permits, that is something that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May the witness please be shown Exhibit S387B.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for the Court's information, we did discover that S387B is the same as S4. And the translation is attached to S4. I don't believe we had the translation for 387.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this information. May I ask Madam Registrar to add this to the list of exhibits. Please be so kind and read this article. And does it reflect the reality?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Should I read everything, or can I just glance over it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Just glance over it, and if you think that --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, just to take a look at it, then. I've read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You yourself are mentioned in person in this article. Once again the question: Does this article from Kozarski Vjesnik, if I'm correct, 24 April 1992 reflect the reality, the political scene in Prijedor, about the elected government of the Serbian Municipality?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reality of the political situation is a broader term, but what it states here, that the government of the Serbian Municipality was elected is something that does correspond to the facts at the time. The people who are mentioned here were elected to these posts, and amongst them I was also elected as the secretary of the secretariat for national defence. In the bottom part of the text, however, I would like to note that I don't know whether it was the journalist or those who prepared the meeting were aware that some of the people who are mentioned on the bottom of this text were elected by the assembly with the approval of the leader of the state body. And the people, the president of the court, the public of the Prosecutor, and the magistrate judge, according to me, they should only have made a draft proposal. And this was something that should have been determined by other bodies. But in the context of how it was put here, yes, those people were elected. And even though a number of those elected were actually in the jurisdiction of some other bodies, so draft proposals were established here, but these other people, Drljaca, Kuruzovic, Goronjic, and the other people who were officials of state bodies could not have been elected by the assembly without prior approval of the leaders of the bodies at the republican level. And I think that the judges were actually under the jurisdiction of the assembly at the republican level. But most of the things that are stated here are true, even though I'm not going into how the journalist understood what is actually stated here. But I'm not disputing the actual text of the article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Just to be not misled by previous testimony, you yourself participated at this meeting Thursday, 16th of April. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was present at the meeting when the executive committee of the Municipal Assembly was elected in this composition. We need to keep in mind the following -- well, if I were to comment on the text as it is, there was never an actual government at the municipal level. So these are some variations which perhaps we shouldn't be spending any time on at this point. But it is something that I wish to point out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We are aware that there are some problems with the terminology, especially when used by journalists. But what was the procedure at this meeting of the Prijedor Serbian Municipality, Thursday, the 16th of April? Were all these persons mentioned here elected in the same way or was there a separation that there was only a proposal for some persons? You mentioned especially Mr. Kuruzovic, Mr. Goronjic, Mr. Kreco, Mr. Tomic, and Mr. Milojica?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I recall those events, relating to myself because probably I was focussed on myself and my own duties, I believe that Mr. Mico Kovacevic addressed the meeting and proposed members for the executive committee. And I think then there was a vote on some kind of ballot. I don't remember exactly what was written on these ballots, and now I don't remember whether Mr. Mico Kovacevic proposed these other people or whether it was someone else. I don't know. I know only that the members of the executive committee were proposed by Mr. Kovacevic, which refers to these people here. But I don't remember who proposed these others and whether they were all on the same ballot or whether these two groups of names were separate. I don't remember that in view of the fact that I wasn't the one who voted, even though I did see this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did the assembly follow all proposals given by Mr. Kovacevic or were there proposals not obtaining the necessary majority?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no other proposals, other than what was proposed by Mr. Kovacevic as far as I recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So in fact, the assembly endorsed all the suggestions made by Dr. Kovacevic. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The suggestions pertaining to members of the executive council, I can state that with certainty. As far as this other part, I did express my reservations about the election or the appointment of those people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Correct. Who could decide on the dismissal from the post of commander of logistics, security?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not a precise term "commander." There was in that sense -- I can perhaps reformulate the question. There was no commander of logistics and security. I don't know of any such term. As part of the 43rd Brigade, there was an assistant commander for logistics. And as part of the 5th Kozara Brigade, there was an assistant commander for logistics. Also, as part of the municipal staff of the TO, which we spoke about earlier, the unit for space and structure, there was also a logistics person. As far as the 43rd Brigade is concerned, the commander of the brigade was the one who decided on that with the approval of his superiors. As far as the TO is concerned, this was done by the commander of the TO, probably with the approval of his superior officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you know a Mr. Iso Bucan?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Mr. Iso -- I don't know Mr. Iso Bucan. I know Mr. Iso Bucan. He worked in the municipal staff of the TO as an assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May the witness be shown Exhibit S26. Could you please comment on this decision.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as regulations go, I've told you already about the competencies and authorities of various bodies. I did not have an opportunity to see this document. I don't remember that this was discussed at the Executive Board or that such a decision was made. If I had been present and if I had been familiar with this issue, I probably would have asked for the action in accordance with the prevailing laws.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So your assessment would be that this would be a decision in judicial terms ultra vires, not within the powers of Dr. Kovacevic. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. The final question as to the Crisis Staff: We heard a lot about the Crisis Staff. We heard a lot about the secretariat for national defence. We heard a lot about Council for National Defence. We heard a lot about TO. And we are aware that related to the acting persons, there was to a certain extent an overlap, especially between counsel for national -- Council for National Defence and Crisis Staff. Could you please be so kind - I know this can't be done within one minute - explain the relationship of these four institutions, and especially the overlap between Council for National Defence on the one hand side and Crisis Staff on the other.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that the Council for National Defence was the advisory body of the Municipal Assembly, and that it was established by the Municipal Assembly and that it is his duty to discuss the issue pertaining to national security and give proposals to the Municipal Assembly relative to these issues. And these competencies are prescribed by the defence law when it comes to the municipality and the authorities of the municipality in that area. So this is a body established by the Municipal Assembly, and it is an advisory body that gives proposals to the Municipal Assembly about the duties and tasks that are to be performed by the Municipal Assembly. And Crisis Staff, on the other hand, is a newly established body which took over the competencies and authorities of the Municipal Assembly. Because in a given situation, the Municipal Assembly could not meet, and in that part, I would rule out the term "overlapping" of authorities or competencies because the Crisis Staff took over the competencies and authorities of the Municipal Assembly, and the National Security Council is a body established by the Municipal Assembly. While the Municipal Assembly existed during the time of peace, it was duty bound to establish that body, but I don't think that it was ever established properly but that the situation called for the -- for a certain body to gather. So Mr. Stakic and Mr. Cehajic remembered that there was a body that gathered all the heads of various sectors, and that's why they started calling the sessions of this National Security Council. At the moment when the Crisis Staff took over the authorities and competencies of the Municipal Assembly, the duties of the Security Council stopped, and for a month or two, while the Crisis Staff existed and National Security Council didn't exist - didn't work that is - only when the situation was stabilized and when the assembly could again meet, after that first session of the assembly, the Security Council continued its work. I don't know whether I should elaborate on the relationship between the Territorial Defence and the municipal secretariat. But I believe that you can find that in documents, and I don't think I should go over and repeat what the regulations say about these authorities. And I've already explained how the heads of these organs are appointed and with whose consent they are appointed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let us now turn to another issue, your concrete work in your secretariat. Did you have files about the persons which were to be mobilised?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. To the first stage, we had complete record for every able-bodied man. Everybody had their own file containing his personal details. And immediately after these events, since I had very few employees, we managed to buy some PCs, and then we kept records on able-bodied men in the computers. That was the official record of that organ for all the able-bodied men between the ages of 16 and 60 and up to 65 for officers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Does the file include personal data on the ethnicity and nationality of a single individual?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The files were comprehensive. All that information was recorded. I believe that there were 25 or 26 different pieces of information. All the personal data including the family status, and where the family was during the previous war, the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So the question is -- the answer is yes, there would be access to the ethnicity and nationality of a single individual?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And did it happen during 1992 that people you wanted to mobilise were regarded as missing?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In terms of the implementation of mobilisation, we had our own files. And then we called up people to the army and other military structures. One of them being work obligation. We did that through our courier service. Mobilisation papers were printed, and couriers would deliver them. And if they couldn't find the person at the specific address, if the conscript was not there, the courier was supposed to make a note of that. He was supposed to say "absent," "not at home," and the courier could not do anything else. He couldn't investigate.
