All he could state was that somebody was not at home, but he could not claim that somebody was missing. He could only state that the conscript, the person who was being called up, could not be found at home at the moment when the delivery of the callup papers were attempted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Were you ever asked or did it spontaneously to print out lists of people based on ethnicity that we would have a list of Serbs, a list of Muslims, a list of Croats?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nobody asked me to do that. That was not done. And I would not have allowed that while I was in my office because it would have been contrary to the law. Laws had to be applied, and I believe that if one applied laws across the board, it makes one's job easier. My job was not easy in any case, and I thought that the only thing that would make it easier was to apply laws equally across the board.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You mentioned just a minute ago the concrete procedure. A person couldn't be found at home. Could you then make the attempt to find out whether such a person would be detained in Omarska, Keraterm, Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In keeping with our regulations, we would send the courier again to the same address. The courier would return with the information whether he found the conscript at that address or not, whether the conscript was willing to be served with the callup papers or not. And that is the only information we got from the courier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So you would never make follow-up attempts to find out where this person actually lives?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not up to me. I was just the head of the body that kept the records on a huge number of conscripts. Calling people and the organisation of couriers, the feedback that the couriers gave us was under the authority of other people. I was just in charge of the legality of all that. There were other people, Serbs and other people who had run away, who failed to respond to the mobilisation. And I don't have any information on who they were, who was it. I just -- I did my job, and there were other people who would inspect the callup papers that the couriers brought back. I was only in charge of the plan. I was asked to prepare the mobilisation paper for a certain number of troops. Whether it's going to be Pero, Petar, Simo, Faruk, or somebody else, I found that absolutely irrelevant. It was my job just to prepare -- according to the plan, prepare the mobilisation of a certain number of troops.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you have, in fact, people enough to -- for the purposes of mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't have enough staff. The requirements of the army and other structures were beyond any needs; that is, at least my opinion. It was their desire to mobilise everybody. There was such a situation in 1992. I was talking about the mobilisation up to April 1992. And then sometime in June, or May or June 1993, the army adopted a territorial principle, and they inspected all the conscripts in villages and towns, and they formed battalions. So every able-bodied person was assigned to a certain job in the army which paralysed the life in the town. And that's why we insisted with the army to give us back some of the professionals, engineers, and other professionals who were essential for maintaining a certain level of life in the town. In any case, we never had as many people as they asked for. This is where the biggest problems arose from. Directors wanted a certain number of men; the army wanted a certain number of men; the police wanted a certain number of men. Some would get killed, some would run away, and they all turned to me to solve their problems. So I was in a very complicated situation, so to speak, between a rock and a hard place. There were pressures on me from all sides. Everybody wanted more men than they could get.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Wouldn't it have been a possibility to mobilise persons detained in one of the collection centres?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not keep any records as to who went where. We just had our records. And according to our records, we sent callup papers. I didn't know where a certain conscript was and what he did. I'm talking about the people who were not mobilised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So there was no attempt from your side to find out based on lists or based on a personal visit that people being detained in Omarska could be mobilised? And then why not?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within the competencies of the organ that I was the head of, I didn't take any actions that would involve the developments and the things that went on in collection centres. I was not in a position to visit any of the collection centres. And let me go back to my job, which I did in accordance with our records and in accordance with the then-prevailing regulations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So it would be your testimony that you never visited one of the detention centres. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. This is what I claim. I have never visited any of the collection centres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What would you call "collection centre" in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the communication that I used, in the correspondence, collection centres were in Omarska, Trnopolje, and Keraterm. They were collection centres or reception centres. Maybe reception centre is a better word for Omarska, Trnopolje, and Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Reception centre. Reception centre. Why do you want to call it reception centre?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, reception centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Normally you use this term in a hotel "reception." Reception for what purpose --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Budimir --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: We used both terms, reception centre, collection centre. If people gathered in a certain place, then it is probably more acceptable to use the term "collection" centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: How many people were killed in these reception or collection centres?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any information on that. I've told you that within my job, I did not take any actions, measures, or procedures to that effect. So I don't know anything about the situation in the collection centres in the territory of the municipality. I don't know whether any people were killed, how many, because my organ never kept any records on that, nor did we take any actions to that effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What about the Prijedor JNA barracks?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The JNA barracks was in the same place where it is to this very day, and it accommodated the troops and part of the command, and there also some of the troops who were not stationed in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Was it used as - using your terminology - as a reception centre, the Prijedor JNA barracks?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I visited the barracks from time to time. Not very often, and when I went there, I did not see any civilians except for conscripts who had been called up. I don't remember that any people were gathered there so as to make the barracks a reception centre in the sense that we were talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What about Ljubija football stadium?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any information about that. Throughout the war, I was in Ljubija only in late 1994 or early 1995 when the troops were moved there. And I believe that it was then that I visited the stadium for the first time throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What about Miska Glava community centre?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that. I don't have any information on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Now, what about the SUP building in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: People were brought in to the SUP building in Prijedor. How many and what people, I don't know. But I know that people were brought to the SUP building where they were taken from there and when, I don't know, because I think it was under the authority of the bodies of the interior, but I did see them bringing in people to the SUP building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you know about detention facilities behind the building as such?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Behind the building, there is an area used as a parking lot, and there's also a restaurant. And within that restaurant, there are two -- there were two rooms or three rooms which had been used as detention or a prison even before these events. And I believe that they took a certain number of people to these rooms. First, they would take them into their offices, and then they would take them to those rooms where there was the restaurant. And these same rooms that were used as detention rooms had existed even before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Who set up the Omarska centre, the Keraterm centre, and the Trnopolje centre?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't have an opportunity to attend a meeting about those centres. I don't have any precise information as to -- under whose orders and based on what authority those centres were established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would it be your testimony here under solemn declaration that the question of these centres or camps was never discussed in the meetings of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am stating that at the meetings which I attended, the Crisis Staff meetings did not discuss the questions or the jurisdictions relating to the collection centres except towards the end. I don't know whether this was in September or October. There was a request from the Red Cross, and I think on that occasion, something was discussed in terms of a departure of a number of the citizens from the collection centre to Trnopolje in accordance with some kind of list by the Red Cross. So something was discussed relating to this matter, and steps were being asked for. I don't know whether our Red Cross was making a request from us or whether it was the International Red Cross. I don't remember. But something along these lines was discussed. I don't know whether it was a meeting of the council or a meeting of the staff. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In the decision on the organisation and work of Prijedor municipal Crisis Staff, Exhibit S180, issue 1, it reads under Article 6, "In discharging its functions in the area of defence, the Crisis Staff shall in particular coordinate the work and activities of all components of all people's defence. Consider issues of mobilisation, development, and reinforcement of the armed forces and other organisations and foster their cooperation with other responsible municipal organs. On special request of the commander of the municipal TO staff, deal with issues of supply requirements and funding sources for the TO. Keep abreast of all aspects of the situation in the municipality essential for the waging of armed combat and take appropriate measures." Wasn't the general purpose of the establishment of a Crisis Staff to maintain or to keep public order in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In accordance with the decision and the instructions and the prerogatives undertaken by the Crisis Staff, the Crisis Staff overtook the functions of the Municipal Assembly and its jurisdictions. So it's normal that the Municipal Assembly deals with all the events on the territory of the municipality relating to law and order. But the Municipal Assembly does not have the organs of power of actually enforcing law and order. And in accordance with the current regulations was not able to order the bodies that are entrusted under the law with preserving law and order. So the Crisis Staff, when they became aware of all of these events, looting, robbery, and other such things, could ask the other organs whose job it was to restore law and order in the territory of the Prijedor Municipality. And I think this is what was actually requested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I'm just trying to follow the line of thoughts of persons having political responsibility in Prijedor Municipality. It is their case that there was a situation of emergency, and therefore a Crisis Staff was established. And wouldn't it then be only consequent that in case there were incidents of, for example, the taking over of power in Prijedor, that those -- from the view maybe of those being responsible in the municipality of Prijedor it would be necessary to arrest and detain purported or alleged criminals, and wouldn't it then be consequent to set up facilities such as Omarska, Keraterm, and Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke here about my position and my political responsibility. The jurisdiction of my body did not include this. This was the police --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I spoke about your participation as a member of a Crisis Staff and whether these issues of public safety and order were discussed in the Crisis Staff, including the situation and the setting up of these camps.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Issues relating to public law and order, and the events that took place in the municipality of Prijedor, I've already said that we discussed that and constantly warned the police and other organs to maintain order and to try to suppress these unlawful acts. The second part of the question, the meetings that I attended, the staff meetings that I attended, there was no discussion about the collection centre, their establishment, the situation in those centres, nor did any organ of the police or military report or submit any reports to the Crisis Staff relating to these issues. I've already said that once there was a request either by the International Red Cross or our local Red Cross in August or September when they requested certain things. I attended that meeting. This related to the departure of certain citizens from the Trnopolje collection centre in response to a request to that effect from the International Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: When meeting, say, with Mr. Drljaca, did you ever discuss in the framework of a meeting of a Crisis Staff or elsewhere the situation that public order could be maintained by setting up such centres?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not have good relations with Mr. Drljaca because of some prior events. I've stated this in my statement to the Prosecution, that as an inspector, I monitored his work while he was in a company in the basic education centre actually. And since the tasks relating to the defence in that domain had quite a lot of importance, and he was not carrying out those duties in an appropriate way, I and another colleague were given instructions for him to be removed from performing those functions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In the moment, your mike doesn't function because I want to ask you to answer my questions, and my question is did Mr. Drljaca report when visiting, you called him yourself as a visitor and not a member of the Crisis Staff. When he visited the Crisis Staff, did he ever discuss with you the issues and the problems emanating from the setting up of these centres?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not talk about that topic with Mr. Drljaca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Who was it, setting up these centres, these camps?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I do not have information or knowledge why and under whose authorisation these collection centres were set up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And based on your education, on that what you learned at university, you were not interested at all what happened in your own community, in the municipality of Prijedor? Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say that. I did not have the opportunity to do so. I was performing the function that I was performing, but in a way I was not a part of that area and the process which relates to those events. It's not that I wasn't interested. I did ask for the establishment of law and order on several occasions. But for the reasons I mentioned, the answer I received from the people from the police was "You're looking for order, you're looking for law. But our people are getting killed here." So that's how it would end. And they did not offer us any solutions because they were much stronger compared to my position, and they were also members of the party. And as such, they enjoyed the confidence of the party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May the witness please be shown Exhibit S107. Could it be zoomed in a way that we can read the entire document. Could you please be so kind and read out --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Excuse me, could the interpreters have a copy of the document because it's hard to see it from the ELMO. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In its entirety" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think for the purposes of today, we only need the top and the first two paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: "With a view to the speedy and effective establishment of the peace on the territory of Prijedor Municipality and in accordance with the decision of the Crisis Staff, I hereby order the following: The industrial compound of the Omarska mine strip mine -- the industrial compound of the Omarska mine strip mine shall serve as a provisional collection centre for persons captured in combat or detained on the grounds of the security services operational information." Under 2: "Together with the appropriate documents, the persons taken into custody shall be handed over to the chief of security, who is duty-bound, in collaboration with the national, public, and military security coordinators, to put them up in any of the five premises allocated for the accommodation of detainees."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Who signed this document?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Chief of public security, Simo Drljaca. That is what I see here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So being aware about this actual situation in Prijedor, and based on the testimony we had previously by numerous witnesses, is it your testimony as you sit here under solemn declaration that this issue was never discussed in the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am stating that this document and these issues were not discussed at the Crisis Staff meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In another document of the Serbian Republic Ministry of the Interior security services, Banja Luka, Document S152, under the heading "reception centres in the municipality," it reads in paragraph 2: "During these conflicts, the army of the Serbian Republic captured many members of hostile formations and other persons who had been in the zones of armed conflicts, and a number of citizens leaving their homes and flats sought help and protection. In order to solve the problem that had arisen, the Crisis Staff of the Municipality of Prijedor decided to organise reception and accommodation in the settlement of Trnopolje for persons who sought protection, and that prisoners of war should be held for processing in the building of the Keraterm RO in Prijedor or in the administrative building and workshop of the iron ore mine in Omarska." So this document issued by the Serbian Republic Ministry of the Interior security services Banja Luka signed by Mr. Bera [phoen], Mr. Kondic, by Mr. Mijic and Mr. Rodic. This would be a flagrant lie when it reads: "The Crisis Staff of Municipality of Prijedor decided to organise all this." They did lie, or who is lying?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff was not the one that decided on that. The part which refers to the actual information and when and the time, as far as I know, based on my work in the Crisis Staff, I believe that the Crisis Staff did not work on that, nor did it adopt such a decision, nor did I ever see any such decision relating to the establishment of collection centres. That information, nor the document that I have before me now was never reviewed by a meeting of the Crisis Staff which I attended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You're aware of my admonition of yesterday, and you clearly understood this. And it will be for you to take -- or to accept the necessary consequences. May the witness please be shown Exhibit S250.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If the witness could be so kind and go through this document, please. You mentioned already in your testimony that the decisions taken by the Crisis Staff were later confirmed by the Municipal Assembly. And now we have this document before us, and if you could be so kind to go through this document and until you find a conclusion of 2nd July, 1992. May I ask Madam Registrar to find the following document. Did you find the decisions of 2nd July 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. It's on page 10, the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If you would be so kind and read out what you can read under XVII and then 4.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Conclusion number 01-023-45/92, prohibiting the individual releases of persons from Trnopolje, Omarska, and Keraterm."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If I'm not wrong, the entire title continues without the approval of the Crisis Staff. Did you ever discuss the individual release of persons from, Omarska, Keraterm and Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: At meetings at the Crisis Staff which I attended, this was not discussed, so I don't know whether this was discussed perhaps at a meeting that I did not attend. But it is the right of the organs entrusted with maintaining law and order to know who the people were there that were taken there and why they were taken there. But this was not something that was in the jurisdiction of the Crisis Staff. And I don't see why this would be discussed at Crisis Staff meetings. This was under the jurisdiction of the security services and the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask the Prosecution, having a database, what is the exhibit number of this document mentioned there, please? In the meantime, may the witness please be shown Document S84.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If I understood Your Honours' question about the decision prohibiting the individual releases of persons from the camps, interestingly, that decision, that actual order, was never seized. It was never found.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The question was, then, in addition, we discussed it previously, when going through the Official Gazette, may I ask the usher to -- or Madam Registrar to hand over to me issue 3 of 1992 of the Official Gazette. But in the meantime, let's concentrate on the document the witness is just reading, another decision of 2nd July. Did you participate in this meeting, the 2nd of July?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember whether I participated at this meeting or not. I didn't have the opportunity to see an order formulated in this way relating to the loss or discontinuation of employment. I know that there were instructions relating to persons who did not respond to the callup or mobilisation in accordance with the law would have their job suspended unless they reported to work within five days. So I did not have anything to do with any issues relating to what is said in this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But isn't it true, Mr. Budimir, that in fact the Crisis Staff of the Prijedor Municipality, 2nd of July 1992, discussed the issue of the termination of the employment of workers "currently in Omarska and Keraterm"?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not disputing the authenticity of this document, but I'm saying that I don't remember whether I attended a session where -- at which this was decided or whether this was decided at any of the sessions that I attended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May the witness be shown, then, Exhibit S90, 9-0. Coming back for a moment to the previous document, S250, there you saw that at the same date following this adoption of decisions taken by the Crisis Staff, apparently this -- on this, the same day, 2nd of July 1992, a decision of the Crisis Staff was taken prohibiting the individual release of persons from Omarska, Keraterm, and Trnopolje. Did you discuss this, because it was the approval of decisions taken by Crisis Staff, all the decisions of Crisis Staff in one decision? Do you recall the discussion of the question of the individual release of persons from Omarska, Keraterm, and Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that we discussed those matters. Maybe I didn't attend that particular session. But if there had been a discussion, then I was not one of the attendants. Or in a different case, this was not discussed. Given my way of work, my profession, my education, my experience, I would have reacted if these issues had been discussed because if one body discusses issues that pertain to the authority of another body, that is wrong. And I don't think that this happened. What I'm saying is that either I didn't attend the session at which this was discussed or the Crisis Staff never discussed these issues at any of its sessions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then finally let's go to these minutes you have before you. Do you recall this meeting of 29 September 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a number of meetings. I will remember things if I attended a meeting. But obviously, some things I will not remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Is it correct that it reads in the beginning, the session was attended by inter alia Slavko Budimir?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Dr. Stakic, Simo Drljaca, Milan Kovacevic, and that it reads on the agenda: "Report on the forthcoming activities regarding the open Trnopolje reception centre"?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask the usher to go to the next page of the same document. Do you recall being present during this meeting? Is it reflected correct that it was in your presence and the session was presided over by the president of the National Defence Council, Dr. Milomir Stakic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So isn't it true that at this occasion, you discussed issues related to Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we were talking, I believe that there was some sort of a discussion about the reception centre in Trnopolje, and one can see that either it was the International Red Cross or the local Red Cross, and you can see that it was decided that these people could leave the reception centre. And I've already said that when it comes to these collection centres, that I attended this meeting and that there was a discussion on the request of either the International Red Cross or the municipal Red Cross for the release of a certain number of persons from this open reception centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So I will have only one additional question immediately after the now-following break, and then as it was custom in the past, because we are now in the Defence case, it would be for the Defence to continue with their questions, and then for the Prosecution to continue. The trial stays adjourned until 5 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Budimir, did you attend meetings with one of the following persons: Ms. Biljana Plavsic, Mr. Karadzic, or Mr. Mladic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't attend meetings together with the persons that you've mentioned, nor I had the opportunity during the performance of my duties and tasks to meet any of these persons. I only met with the defence minister.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And the name of the defence minister at that time was, please?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Bogdan Subotic, and after him, Mr. Kovacevic. After Mr. Kovacevic, Mr. Ninkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And what was the issue you discussed with the minister of defence?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the minister came to Prijedor for the first time, I didn't discuss any of the concrete issues. We, rather, talked with the families of the fallen soldiers, and invalids, so we had meetings with those families in the big hall of the municipal building. These were the issues that we discussed because this was something that was added to our scope of duties, the burials of soldiers and those who were killed in all sorts of incidents and accidents and other such things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Same question related to meetings or contacts with General Momir Talic, Mr. Stojan Zupljanin, Mr. Krajisnik? Did you ever meet one of these persons? Did you have contact with one of these persons?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't have contacts with any of the persons you have mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. May I ask you whether one of the following issues would fall into the area of your competence: The formation of a committee to receive captured goods?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The recruitment of persons born in 1974?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The obligation for the secretariat for economic affairs regarding salaries?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Recognising time served in the Serbian Territorial Defence and the police as time spent in military training?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence and the police, yes, that was one of the competencies of my body. All the recognition of the participation and administrative procedures relative to the defence was under the authority of my body.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The coordination of wartime disposition of the military and police?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. My organ did not coordinate anything. It only worked according to rules and regulations. We were not a coordinator between the army and the police. We only carried out mobilisation of personnel and materiel and technical equipment. We did not have the role of a coordinator in those things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The obligation to pay military and police members, you mentioned, and the request to the Red Cross to check the possibility of interested persons crossing over into Croatia via Bosanska Dubica?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are two different issues. Could you please take each of them at a time so I can focus on them separately. The first question, the salaries, my secretariat did not have any authority in that area. As for the second part of your question, in keeping with the decree on the movement of goods and military conscripts, we issued permits for the movements of conscripts and citizens in the territory of the republic and outside of the territory of the republic. That is what my body did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you recall the discussion within the Crisis Staff of the recruitment of persons born in 1974?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. But I don't think that there was any need for the Crisis Staff to discuss that because it was under the authority of a certain organ, and there was no need to discuss it at great length. This was a prescribed duty that was under the authority of my body, of my secretariat. So there was no need for us to discuss anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I mentioned these points, these three points, where you stated that this would fall under your area of responsibility. These were enactments passed by the Crisis Staff on 2nd July 1992 and confirmed the 24th of July 1992 by the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor. So in fact, enactments of the Crisis Staff on this 2nd of July 1992. To be even more concrete, these enactments passed this 2nd of July 1992, these previous decisions, they were presented to the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor by a document of 24 July 1992, that is, Exhibit S250, and then the decision followed that "All acts" -- emphasise "All acts (decisions, orders, rulings, and conclusions) adopted by the Crisis Staff of the Municipality of Prijedor or the war presidency between 29 May and 24 July 1992 are hereby ratified." Dr. Milomir Stakic, signed. Date 27 August 1992, Official Gazette, year 1, Monday, 31 August 1992, number 3 of 1992, Exhibit S181. So apparently on this 2nd of July 1992, three enactments passed the Crisis Staff in your area of responsibility following your own testimony. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask the usher once again to present Document S250, and XVII. I don't know whether the pagination in B/C/S is the same as in English, but in English, it would be page 9. And 10 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise again. I don't see it in front of me. I don't have it in front of me. I can't find it in any case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] XVII --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honour, microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've found the XVII.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: At the bottom of page 10 B/C/S, and continuing at the top of page 11.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, conclusion under 2, salaries; under 3, requesting the Red Cross to check the possibility of interested persons crossing to -- crossing into Croatia via Bosanska Dubica. In this specific case, I've already told you that we issued permits in keeping with the decree. And it says here that possibility should be checked for the interested person to cross, but this was not under my authority. It was under my authority to issue certificates and permits, and the recognition of the time spent in the Territorial Defence under military training, I said that this was in keeping with legal regulations that were prevalent at the time. The issue of the military exercise was under the authority of the secretariat for the defence. And here, the conclusion on the intake of the year 1974, those born in 1974, this was also under the authority of the secretariat of defence. Maybe this was just information or -- I can't really say what this is exactly. But this was under the authority of the secretariat of defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And then, please, issue number 5.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You also testified previously that this would fall in the area of your responsibility.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And the same is true with number 7?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Does this now refresh your recollection whether or not you were present during this Crisis Staff meeting the 2nd of July 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If these issues were discussed, that doesn't mean that I attended this session. I can't tell you whether I attended this session or not because these issues were not of any significance for the organ that I was affiliated with, save for the recruitment. But I believe that this issue was just given in the form of information on the number of conscripts who were recruited throughout the year. I believe that just information was given, but this does not help me recollect, doesn't help me remember whether I attended this particular session or whether I participated in the discussion at that particular session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let us now see, please, video Exhibit S240. And before we start, please distribute the transcript, S240, I believe it must be -1. I think it starts on page 3 of the transcript, but we can hear it both in English and B/C/S, I think. So please, start the video now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: [Please refer to Exhibit S187-1 for video transcript]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. You may stop the video here. Having heard this by Dr. Stakic in person, that these centres "were established by the civilian government," having seen the enactments, having seen the decisions, having heard about the report of the Serbian Republic Ministry of the Interior stating that the Crisis Staff of the Municipality of Prijedor decided to organise reception documentation in Trnopolje, Keraterm, and Omarska, Mr. Budimir, is it still your testimony that these issues were never discussed in the Crisis Staff in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I claim with full responsibility that at the sessions of the Crisis Staff that I attended, there was no decision passed on the establishment of these investigation or collection centres. Also, I claim that the issues pertaining to the authority of these centres were never discussed. If the president who stated so in his statement did so, under what authority, on whose orders, he never said that at any of the sessions of the Crisis Staff in full composition. Whether this was a product of some sort of relationship between Mr. Stakic, Mr. Drljaca, and Mr. Kovacevic, whether some things have been imposed on him from those circles to state what he did, I don't know. In any case, I never attended any sessions where this was discussed and where decisions would be made on anything pertaining to collection centres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So you feel misinformed by the at that time president?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the sessions where we discussed issues, I was informed. But as for the communication between the president and his superiors, Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Arsic, Mr. Simo and these relationships, I was not informed, and I don't have any information about communication at that level, about discussions among those peoples. I was not informed about that, so I cannot say anything about that segment of that work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What brings you to the conclusion that Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Arsic, and Mr. Simo were the superiors of Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that they were his superiors. I believe President Karadzic was his superior in terms of coordination. And the others were his associates or collaborators, each of them in their segment of work. But I've already said that they socialised more. They spent more time together. And I don't know what they discussed informally. At the official sessions of the Crisis Staff that I was a member of, these issues were not discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What does it mean "superior in terms of coordination"?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say "superiors in terms of coordination." In terms of coordination, there was no superiority relationship.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I quote from your answer, and I will repeat. This is on page 68, line 9. "I didn't say they were his superiors. I believe President Karadzic was his superior in terms of coordination."

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is what I said. I said that President Karadzic was his superior, but not Mr. Arsic or Mr. Drljaca. I said that it was Mr. Karadzic who was his superior and that by the line of command on the subordination, it was Mr. Karadzic who delivered documents to Dr. Stakic, one of the documents being the establishment of the Crisis Staff. So I believe that this was the line of communication, and this was the only vertical line of communication that was in keeping with the then prevailing regulations. I believe that it was the president of the state who delivered certain documents to the president of the Municipal Assembly. In the same way, the minister of defence handed down documents to me, in the same way, I believe, that documents were handed down from the president of the state to presidents of various municipalities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Finally, on page 67, line 12, you made the following statement: "I claim with full responsibility that at the sessions of the Crisis Staff that I attended, there was no decision passed on the establishment of these investigation or collection centres. Also, I claim that these issues pertaining to the authority of these centres were never discussed." The question still is, was there ever any discussion related to those centres or camps, not only related to the establishment but to the fact that in the Prijedor Municipality, there were these centres or camps? Was this discussed in the Crisis Staff or not?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the sessions of the Crisis Staff, we never heard the information or report either from the police or the army who provided security there. So in a formal form, in an official form, in terms of report or information, there was never discussion on any of these issues at a session of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. For me it's enough for the moment. Judge Vassylenko, please. Sorry, now it's the wrong order. In this case, Judge Argibay, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Budimir, I have a couple of questions for you. Because I'm very surprised at your election as a secretary for defence in the Serbian government of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor because you told us, am I right, that you were not a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true, I was not a member of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: In what capacity were, then, you asked to be a part of this government set up by the SDS?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view, I worked in that body, and as part of the structures within the SDS and in a way, all the other posts were filled more easily, they didn't have a proposal because the activities of that organ and the time available as well as the fact that this happened to be the most difficult situation relating to the work of that organ, that they had to send people for military duty, that there were daily casualties almost because I would have to go to at least two families a day to tell them that one of their relatives, their father, brother, husband was killed. So the people in the SDS, none of the people there wanted to accept that post. And when the time had run out, the deadline had expired, then they presented me with a deadline to decide within a period of two days, to decide whether I wanted to take that post or not. And at that time, there was already a lot of dissension and disagreement between the three ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: And why did you accept that very difficult, not-likable place?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me say that at that point, I didn't have any choice. After the announcement was made, frankly speaking, I was in two minds about it for two days, and I talked about this with my closest friends and with my brother. But there was no way of going back, you know, because on one side, the population had divided; on one side, there were the Muslims, and on the other side were the Serbs. Had I not accepted that post, I would have been declared a traitor of my people and I would have been abused by those people. So I was in the situation since I was already in that organ simply to continue with my work and to try to base that work as much as possible on prevailing laws and regulations and to make sure that what we did was in respect of the law if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: But you stayed after the takeover.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that -- I said that I was appointed to that post, and I continued to perform those functions until the end of the war. After the war ended, I left that position and I went away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Okay. I still don't understand why you accepted the first time, but then you stayed over after the takeover in Prijedor. That's correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I accepted for the reasons that I stated. And I remained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Well, you are speaking all the time that you are staying or you were staying at the office because you wanted to do the things lawful. Wasn't the takeover an unlawful movement at that moment?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not claim that it was not an unlawful act, but in my previous statements and explanations to the Presiding Judge, I explained the preceding events and the things that happened in the territory of the Prijedor Municipality. So this event cannot be viewed outside of the context of the time period and the events. In the context of how you put the question, without any connection with the rest of the events, it probably does seem that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Wasn't it -- the takeover, wasn't it a coup to displace the legally elected authorities?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you allow me, I would like to say something. I, as a person who worked for a long time in the state organs and who applied the law, from the time of the elections in 1990 when they came to power, the nationalist parties took over, no regulation or law was applied. I understand that if new people come to power and if they need to change regulations, then they should do that. But I cannot understand that the people who are in power while there are existing regulations do not apply those regulations. So from that standpoint, the takeover of power was not something that I could conceive of and all the events that followed. But I, as a person who was caught up in those events, was a person who had a role in all of these events such as it was. I did not participate in political events. And the things that I did do, I tried to do them in accordance with the laws and regulations that were in force at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't have any more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Judge Vassylenko, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Mr. Budimir, I would like to ask you two technical questions. First one: About the status and position of Spiro Marmat. Who was Spiro Marmat? He was expert of the technical service responsible for taking records during the meetings of people's defence council and Crisis Staff, or he was the secretary of the people's defence council?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Spiro Marmat, if you're interested in that part, I can give you more details, he was a person who was carrying out the duties of the secretary of the secretariat for national defence before I did and before two other people who had fulfilled their mandate. He had performed that function to which I was elected before. After 1990, and after the arrival of the nationalist parties took power, he remained in some capacity as deputy to the previous two persons who did it, Dzihic and Abdulah. When Mr. Gottvald was appointed deputy, then the two of them remained as kind of technical or expert advisors in the body. But their posts were not specifically defined. My post was specifically defined. So when the secretariat held its meetings, not I, as a secretary of that organ, but Mr. Marmat, who had performed that post in earlier mandates, was a person who had sufficient experience to take down the minutes and to make sure that they were as correct as possible. So this is actually what he did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The next question: You mentioned -- you told us that the Crisis Staff had 24-hour duty call. And with this purpose, the centre for alerting, collecting, and processing information was set up. And you also called this centre as reporting centre. I would like to know what was the proper, official name of this body.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The official name of that body was the early warning reporting centre, and it was not established at the same time that the Crisis Staff was established. The centre existed before that and existed in peacetime, and its duties were clearly defined. At the point in time when the Crisis Staff was established, the reporting centre was placed in the function of a centre for receiving and processing of information from the civilian sector, based on all the events in the municipality of Prijedor. And those information -- that information was received 24 hours a day in the centre. For example, there was a power cut or the water supply was cut off and so on. Similar events that happened in the town. When we're talking about the economic life, I think there is a document which we had prepared listing the duties of that organ in terms of that. I cannot repeat all of those things, but I think this document exists somewhere there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: My next question: When the work obligations were introduced in Prijedor Municipality, before the takeover or after the takeover? Before the Crisis Staff was set up or after that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The work obligation in the terminological sense is as follows: We allocated some people to the military, some to the police, some to companies or institutions. All the persons who were allocated based on the war assignments to companies were on the schedule as being on work duty. When decisions of higher bodies were adopted, that these companies should switch to a wartime production, then this schedule was moved to their -- as their war assignment. And then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember specifically. But I think it was in the May/June time period, but I can't give you a specific date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Was it the first half of May or the second half of May?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not able to say. I really do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And my last question: You were shown Exhibit S250 which in this document, the decisions and other enactments are listed, decisions and enactments which were adopted by the Crisis Staff between 29 May and 24 July 1992. And here in this document, we have 19 sections. Documents enumerated in Sections 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, and 11 was passed on 3rd, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9, 10, 11, 12 June. Does it mean that the Crisis Staff had its sessions every day at this period of time?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what I remember, this schedule of activities does not accord with the actual state of affairs. I believe that the staff did not have so many sessions. But I would like to restrict that to the way things I remember. As far as I recall, the staff did not have daily meetings. I don't think that there were as many sessions, if I recall that rightly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: May I just for the record, Your Honour, I believe the video that was played was S187. I think it was identified in the transcript as S240 or 246. It was actually S187 that was played, I believe. And that's the video of Dr. Stakic's interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This can be clarified immediately. Thank you for your assistance. We have to continue with the testimony tomorrow. And as to the fact that apparently the testimony takes longer than envisaged, the first steps have already been made in order to enable us to sit maybe 90 minutes longer tomorrow and the day after that. This has to be confirmed no doubt by interpreters and Registrar and all others having to do this work. So only for the parties, please be prepared that it might be we sit longer tomorrow. And as for Dr. Stakic, also the necessary preparations have been made that in case he arrives late, he gets his warm meal and, of course, access to the fresh air as foreseen under the rules. Mr. Lukic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I just wanted to ask the Chamber, do we have to bring a second witness for this week?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think that there is not the slightest problem because the testimony of Mr. Travar, in all likelihood, will not take more than one day. You will see why. So please, kind enough that you ask, but please stick to the schedule.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The same rules apply for you, Mr. Budimir, also for today: No contact with any of the parties and witnesses. So please, come back tomorrow. We are sitting tomorrow at 9.00 in Courtroom number I. This concludes today's hearing. The trial stays adjourned until tomorrow, 9.00.
